title: What first foods are really for
byline: In the second half of the first year, food is there for iron, energy, and learning to eat. It is not about hitting a protein percentage.
image_alt: Minced meat with broccoli and cooked apple

findings.lead: Iron is the first nutrient to run low.
findings.text: Healthy babies born at term have iron stores that last about six months. After that, milk alone can’t keep up.

findings.lead: Babies don’t need twice an adult’s share of protein.
findings.text: More protein in a baby’s diet is linked with faster weight gain, not better development.
Under two, full-fat dairy and a spoonful of oil are the right choice. Low-fat products are for older children and adults.

findings.lead: Fruit purée alone isn’t a meal plan.
findings.text: A plate needs an iron-rich food, a vegetable, and enough energy. Fruit is a welcome extra, not the meal.

sections.heading: Iron
paragraphs: By about six months, the iron stores built up before birth are running down just as your baby is growing fast. Breast milk is still valuable, but it has little iron. That’s why meat, lentils, beans, tofu, and iron-fortified cereal belong in the first weeks of solids, not after a long run of fruit and vegetables.

Vitamin C from fruit or vegetables at the same meal helps the body absorb iron from plants. Tea with meals does the opposite. A baby drinking enough infant formula already gets iron from it, but food still matters: it builds eating skills and the diet that follows the first year.

sections.heading: What about protein?
paragraphs: Adult diets are often described as about 12 to 15 percent protein by energy. Doubling that for a child would mean roughly a quarter of all calories from protein. That is not the infant target. Mature breast milk is closer to 5 to 8 percent protein by energy, and formula is deliberately kept in a modest range.

A randomised trial of infant formula found that more protein led to faster weight gain up to age two. Professional guidance takes this as a reason not to chase protein. Meat and pulses earn their place for iron, zinc, and texture, and because children learn to like them. Not for pushing the protein percentage up.

sections.heading: Fat and energy
paragraphs: The brain is still developing, and meals are small. A teaspoon of rapeseed or olive oil on a purée, or a little full-fat yogurt or pasteurised cheese, adds energy without salt. Low-fat milk and yogurt can wait until after the second birthday.
Flaxseed oil goes rancid quickly and shouldn’t be heated. You don’t need a pricey special oil blend. One ordinary oil, stirred in after cooking, is enough.

sections.heading: What goes on a good plate
paragraphs: A simple pattern that works: one iron-rich food, one vegetable, one familiar starch or fruit, and a little fat. Pumpkin, apple, pear, and banana are lovely but low in iron. Serve them alongside the iron food, not instead of it for weeks on end.
Across a varied week, plant proteins provide all the amino acids a baby needs. Not every meal has to include meat.

title: When to start
byline: The right window opens after four months and runs to about six. Readiness is about skills, but there is still a minimum age.
image_alt: A small bowl of green vegetable purée

findings.lead: Not before 17 weeks, and not much later than six months.
findings.text: European gastroenterology guidance sets that lower limit and asks families not to wait beyond about 26 weeks.

findings.lead: Look for sitting, a steady head, and hands to mouth.
findings.text: Interest in food and a fading tongue-thrust reflex are part of the same picture. Age alone isn’t a signal to start, and neither are these skills before 17 weeks.

findings.lead: Hungarian and European advice are close, but not identical.
findings.text: In Hungary you’ll often hear ‘wait until six months’. The European position allows a start from 17 weeks if the baby is ready, and still wants solids under way by six months.

sections.heading: The window
paragraphs: The World Health Organization supports exclusive breastfeeding for about six months, and that’s the right default for a healthy baby born at term who is growing well. ESPGHAN’s 2017 position is slightly wider: don’t start before four months (17 weeks), and don’t wait beyond six months (26 weeks), because iron and energy needs rise and delaying allergenic foods has no benefit.

EFSA’s 2019 review found no harm for healthy term babies in Europe from starting anywhere in that window. That’s not a reason to aim for four months. It is a reason not to worry if a ready baby starts a few weeks before six months.

sections.heading: Signs to watch for
paragraphs: Look for a baby who can sit with support and hold their head steady, reaches for food and gets it into their mouth, and no longer pushes every spoonful straight back out. These skills protect the airway and make eating possible.
Waking at night, watching you eat, or chewing their fists are ordinary baby behaviours, and not good reasons to start. Nor is hoping it will help them sleep. First foods aren’t a sleep method.

sections.heading: What you will hear in Hungary
paragraphs: Hungary’s 2019 professional guideline on feeding healthy infants (identifier 001038) says solids may start from the beginning of the fifth month and should be under way by about six months. Exclusive breastfeeding to six months still fits within that, and many health visitors put it that way.

Some familiar charts still follow a slow ladder: fruit and vegetables first, then grains, then meat. The evidence on iron and allergy doesn’t support it. Start when your baby is ready, around six months, and include iron and the common allergens from the beginning.

title: Spoon, fingers, or both
byline: Purées, finger foods, or a mix of both can all feed a baby well. The debate about which camp you’re in is louder than the evidence.
image_alt: Smooth carrot purée beside soft roasted carrot strips

findings.lead: Iron, texture, and following your baby’s cues matter more than the method.
findings.text: You can spoon-feed, let your baby feed themselves soft pieces, or do both in the same week.

findings.lead: In a trial that taught safe shapes, finger foods didn’t increase choking.
findings.text: Gagging was common. Choking wasn’t more common when families were shown which shapes to avoid.

findings.lead: Smooth food has a use-by date.
findings.text: By eight or nine months, a baby should be moving on to mashed food and soft pieces. Staying on thin purée is a risk you can avoid.

sections.heading: Three ways that work
paragraphs: Spoon-feeding lets you offer iron-rich meat and lentils in a smooth form while chewing is still new. Finger foods let your baby practise gripping and set their own pace. Most families end up mixing the two, and that’s a proper method in its own right, not a compromise.

As a slogan, baby-led weaning sometimes forgets iron, or keeps meals so simple that the baby fills up on fruit. The studies that found baby-led feeding safe told families to include iron-rich foods and to avoid round, hard, and coin-shaped pieces.

sections.heading: What the BLISS trial showed
paragraphs: New Zealand’s BLISS trial (Baby-Led Introduction to Solids) compared supported baby-led feeding with usual spoon-feeding. There was no sign of more choking. Gagging, which is noisy and protective, was a normal part of learning.

That doesn’t mean every hard shop-bought biscuit is safe. It means soft strips, flakes of fish, and well-cooked vegetables, offered to a baby sitting upright, carried about the same risk as spoon-feeding.

sections.heading: Keep moving the texture on
paragraphs: At first, food can be smooth or naturally soft. By about eight months, move to mash with soft lumps and pieces your baby can hold in their fist. By about a year, they should be eating family textures, with their portion still unsalted.

You don’t need a blender. A fork will mash banana, avocado, and the soft inside of baked vegetables. Blenders whip air into food; if your baby seems windy afterwards, stir the purée and let it stand for a bit before serving.

title: Choosing ingredients
byline: Variety, bitter greens included, matters more than an organic label. Only a short list of foods is genuinely unsuitable.
image_alt: Pumpkin, apple, egg, lentils, salmon, and yogurt

findings.lead: Offer bitter and savoury flavours early.
findings.text: Babies who try green vegetables in the first weeks of solids are more willing to eat them later.

findings.lead: Put an iron-rich food on your first shopping list.
findings.text: The practical sources are meat, lentils, beans, tofu, and fortified baby cereal.

findings.lead: A short list of foods to avoid is enough.
findings.text: Honey, added salt, added sugar, rice drinks, whole nuts, unpasteurised dairy, and a few kinds of fish are the ones with a real reason behind them.

sections.heading: Variety, including the tricky flavours
paragraphs: ESPGHAN recommends a range of flavours and textures, bitter greens included. A month of nothing but sweet pear and banana teaches a narrow palate. Broccoli, spinach mixed into something, beans, and fish can all appear in the first two weeks.

Organic produce hasn’t been shown to change allergy or growth in babies. Wash it, and peel it if the skin is tough or very dirty. Eating in season is a pleasure and saves money, but it isn’t a safety rule.

sections.heading: Build around iron
paragraphs: It helps to keep one iron-rich food ready: cooked mince in the freezer, red lentils in the cupboard, unsalted beans, eggs, or a fortified cereal whose taste you can live with. Serve plant iron with fruit or pepper for vitamin C.
Rice cereal is optional. It isn’t needed for sleep or as a first spoonful, and rice drinks are a different product altogether. Children under five shouldn’t have rice drinks, because of arsenic.

sections.heading: Foods to skip or change, and why
paragraphs: Honey, even baked, can contain spores that cause infant botulism. It waits until after the first birthday, and even then it’s still sugar. Salt waits too: a baby’s daily limit is under 1 gram, which ordinary foods already provide, so none is added, and stock cubes, ham, and soy sauce stay out. Sugar and fruit juice aren’t needed; give the fruit itself.

Whole nuts, whole grapes, popcorn, and hard dried fruit are choking hazards. Shark, swordfish, and marlin contain too much mercury. Unpasteurised milk and mould-ripened cheeses can carry listeria. Undercooked kidney beans and other dried beans can make you ill quickly; boil them until completely soft. Liver is nutritious, but so high in vitamin A that one small portion a week is the limit.

title: Cooking and seasoning
byline: Herbs, a mild spice, and a spoonful of oil do more for a baby’s food than salt or sugar ever will.
image_alt: A vegetable stew with parsley, sweet paprika, and oil

findings.lead: No added salt before one year.
findings.text: That includes the cooking water, the stock, and the ‘pinch’ in a pasta sauce.
Added sugar is unnecessary before two years, and honey is unsafe before one.

findings.lead: Cook for the family, then season the grown-ups’ plates.
findings.text: Take out your baby’s portion before salt, chilli, or a salty sauce goes in.

sections.heading: Salt
paragraphs: A baby’s kidneys can’t handle much sodium, and salty food builds a taste for salt that’s hard to undo. The simple rule: no salt in cooking for a child under one. Cheese, bread, and tinned foods already contain some, so keep those to small amounts.
Stock cubes, gravy, ham, bacon, soy sauce, and most ‘baby seasonings’ that list salt are grown-up shortcuts. Your own unsalted stock, frozen in cubes, is a different thing entirely.

sections.heading: Sugar, honey, and spice
paragraphs: Added sugar pushes out iron-rich foods and feeds tooth decay as soon as teeth come through. Fruit, roasted pumpkin, and ripe banana are sweet enough for biscuits and porridge. Honey isn’t a more natural choice under one: botulism spores survive ordinary baking.

Sweet paprika, turmeric, cumin, oregano, basil, and a pinch of cinnamon are all fine. Hot chilli and lots of black pepper are not. Keep cinnamon to a pinch, not a spoonful: cassia cinnamon contains coumarin.

sections.heading: One pot for everyone
paragraphs: Stews, sauces, and roasts can feed the whole household if you lift out the baby’s share first. Mash theirs or cut it to a texture they can manage. Then salt yours.
Garlic and onion cooked into the dish are fine. Garlic or herbs kept in a jar of oil are not: that’s a known botulism risk. Add fresh herbs and oil at the end of cooking.

title: Tools, hygiene, and the freezer
byline: A knife, a pan, and good fridge habits matter more than a drawer full of baby gadgets.
image_alt: Bowls, a saucepan, and frozen herb cubes

findings.lead: You can do without most special baby gear.
findings.text: Replace a scratched non-stick pan. Keep a separate board for raw meat. A fork is enough to mash first foods.

findings.lead: Cool quickly, keep for two days, reheat once.
findings.text: Rice is stricter: cool it within an hour and eat it within a day of refrigerating.

findings.lead: Freeze in portions, and never refreeze.
findings.text: An ice-cube tray of unsalted sauce is more useful than a raw herb paste kept for a week.

sections.heading: What you actually need
paragraphs: You can cook every recipe here with a knife, a chopping board, a saucepan, a frying pan with an undamaged surface, and a blender or a fork. A steamer basket is nice to have. An apple grater isn’t safer than cooked apple for a new eater: raw gratings are uneven and easy to inhale.

If a non-stick coating is damaged, replace the pan rather than keep using it. Raw meat needs its own board, washed in hot water afterwards. Plastic boxes are fine if they’re undamaged and made for food.

sections.heading: Food hygiene for little ones
paragraphs: Cool cooked food within one to two hours in shallow containers, then put it in the fridge. Eat refrigerated meals within two days. Reheat until steaming hot all the way through, stir to get rid of cold spots, then let it cool until it’s safe to eat. Reheat only once. Anything left on your child’s plate is finished; it doesn’t go back in the pot.

Rice and other grains can grow Bacillus cereus if left sitting warm. Cool them within an hour and use refrigerated rice within 24 hours. Boil dried beans hard. Cook eggs for babies until both the white and the yolk are set. Use pasteurised dairy only.

sections.heading: Cooking ahead
paragraphs: Freeze leftover sauce, mince, and purée in small cubes on the day you cook them, and write the date on them. Thaw in the fridge and use within 24 hours, or thaw in the microwave and serve straight away. Once thawed, don’t refreeze.
A raw vegetable and herb paste kept in the fridge for a week is a poor way to store it. The same mixture frozen straight away is a good one. Salt isn’t a preservative you can use here.
